Beaks and Flippers

How Beak Shape and Wing Structure Vary Across Penguin Genera

Author

Beaky Blinders: Andrew King, Maria Sans-Fuentes, Stephanie Wu

Introduction

This project uses the “Many Penguins” dataset, featured in TidyTuesday on 2026-07-14 (week 28) and curated by Ben Bolker of McMaster University. It was created as a richer alternative to the Palmer Penguins dataset that includes only 3 species. Many Penguins dataset contains the penguins (Spheniscidae) records from the much larger AVONET database, a global database of morphological, ecological and geographical traits for nearly all bird species (Tobias et al., 2022). The dataset includes 10 distinct morphometric measurements (physical body measurements) for 93 penguins from 18 species within 6 genera. It is cross-sectional and includes measurements of present-day penguin species, which provides a snapshot of penguins today rather than a record of their changes over time. Sample sizes differ widely among genera, and some measurements are missing for several penguins, especially the hand-wing index, which was missing for 20 penguins (Table 1).

We selected thos dataset because it lets us explore a question inspired by evolution: do closely related groups that share the same lifestyle end up with similar physical traits? Our goal is to describe and compare how beak shape and wing structure differ between the various penguin genera, and whether different genera remain physically distinct despite sharing an aquatic lifestyle.

# Variables used in the analyses
analysis_vars <- c("beak.length_culmen", "beak.length_nares", "beak.width", "beak.depth", "tarsus.length", "hwi")

# Missing values in the beak measurements, by genus
missing_by_genus <- penguins %>%
  group_by(genus) %>%
  summarise(penguins = n(),
            # sum NAs per measurement variable
            across(all_of(analysis_vars), ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
            # sum all the unknown sex values
            sex_unknown = sum(sex == "U"))

                    "Hand-wing index", "Unknown sex")) %>%
    kable_styling() %>%

Question 1: Do penguin genera differ in beak shape?

Introduction

For this question we explore if penguins from the same genus have similar beak shapes that set them apart from other genera, and which part of the beak contributes most to these differences. The dataset includes four beak measurements: beak length (using two different measures), beak width, and beak depth. Together, they give a good picture of overall beak shape. We also use genus to group the penguins and tarsus length as a proxy for body size, so we can check whether differences in beak shape remain once size is removed. Moreover, since beak shape is closely related to diet and how an animal feeds, looking at these differences across genera may suggest how each group has adapted to find food in the ocean.

Approach

We used Principal Component Analysis (PCA)1 on three beak measurements: culmen length, beak width and beak depth, using only penguins with all three measurements (complete cases; see Table 1 and the Analysis section for how we handled missing values). We log-transformed the measurements, which is standard for allometric data2 (Glazier, 2021), and scaled them so that no single measurement had too much weight. To check whether differences between genera were mainly due to size, we also ran the PCA on size-corrected data, using the residuals from regressing each log beak measurement on log tarsus length (a proxy for body size). Because the sign of a PC is arbitrary, we reversed PC1 and PC2 in the size-corrected PCA so that both analyses point in the same direction. Because PCA does not quantify how well genera are separated, we also used a linear discriminant analysis (LDA)3 with leave-one-out cross-validation4 on both the original and the size-corrected measurements.

The bar chart of the loadings (Figure 1) shows how much each beak measurement contributes to each PC. A bar chart is well suited for this because the lengths of the bars can be compared along a common scale, which is easy to read accurately (Cleveland & McGill, 1984), so the measurement that drives each PC stands out. Figure 2 shows two PCA biplots, one above the other: the original PCA and the size-corrected PCA. Each biplot is a scatterplot of the PC scores of each penguin, with genera identified by a color-blind-friendly palette and a different symbol, so they can be told apart without relying on color alone. Arrows are overlaid to show the loadings: each arrow points in the direction in which that beak measurement increases, so penguins located towards an arrow tend to have larger values of that measurement, and longer arrows indicate measurements that are better represented by the two PCs shown. Combined, the points and arrows show whether penguins of the same genus cluster and which measurements explain these clusters.

Analysis

Show the code 
# OWNER: Maria
# Numbers for inline code in the Approach
r_nares         <- cor(penguins$beak.length_culmen, penguins$beak.length_nares,
                       use = "complete.obs")
n_nares_missing <- sum(is.na(penguins$beak.length_nares))
n_depth_missing <- sum(is.na(penguins$beak.depth))

# Missing nares lengths and sample size for the two most affected genera
eudyptula <- missing_by_genus %>% filter(genus == "Eudyptula")
pygoscelis <- missing_by_genus %>% filter(genus == "Pygoscelis")

# keep penguins with all 3 beak measurements 
# Vector with the variable names of the four beak measurements 
pca_vars <- c("beak.length_culmen","beak.width", "beak.depth")

# Number of species

# Data frame for analyses: completecases and log transformation 
pca_dta <- penguins %>%
    # select variables for PCA analysis
    select(all_of(pca_vars), genus) %>%
    # just keep coplete cases
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    # log-transform the three beak measurements
    mutate(across(all_of(pca_vars), log, .names = "log_{.col}"))

# Vector with the log transformed variable names
pca_vars_log <- c("log_beak.length_culmen","log_beak.width", "log_beak.depth")

Before running the PCA, we explored missing values in the four beak measurements (Table 1). While culmen length and beak width were complete, beak depth was missing for 1 penguin, and nares length was missing for 15 penguins, with the highest proportions in Eudyptula (3 of 7) and Pygoscelis (5 of 17). Because nares length was strongly correlated with culmen length (r = 0.85), which also measures beak length, we excluded this measure to avoid losing these penguins. We considered imputing their values, but imputation would add little new information and could make genera appear more distinct than they are. Therefore, we ran the PCA on culmen length, beak width and beak depth, using only penguins with all three measurements (complete cases, n = 92).

Show the code 
# OWNER: Maria (original PCA)
# PCA o the log transformed 3 measurements variables (not size-corrected)
pca_orig <- prcomp(pca_dta[,pca_vars_log], scale=T) 

# Percentage of variance explained by each PC
var_pc <- summary(pca_orig)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100

# Summary of the explained variance per component
summ_pca_var_nonsize <- summary(pca_orig)$importance

# Loadings of the PCs
summ_pca_load_nonsize <- pca_orig$rotation
Show the code 
# OWNER: Stephanie (size-corrected PCA)
# residuals of each log beak measurement on log(tarsus_length)
# Log-transform the beak measurements and tarsus length.
pca_size_dta <- penguins %>%
    select(all_of(pca_vars), tarsus.length, genus) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c(pca_vars, "tarsus.length")), log, .names = "log_{.col}"))

# Regress each log beak measurement on log tarsus length.
size_lm <- lm(as.matrix(pca_size_dta[, pca_vars_log]) ~ log_tarsus.length,
              data = pca_size_dta)

# Take the residuals: what's left of each beak measurement after removing 
# the part explained by body size.
beak_resid <- resid(size_lm)

# Run the PCA on the residuals.
pca_size <- prcomp(beak_resid, scale. = TRUE)

# Flip PC1 and PC2 signs (arbitrary in PCA) so panel B reads like panel A
pca_size$x[, 1:2]        <- -pca_size$x[, 1:2]
pca_size$rotation[, 1:2] <- -pca_size$rotation[, 1:2]

# Percentage of variance explained by each PC
var_pc_size <- summary(pca_size)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100

# Summary of the explained variance per component
summ_pca_var_size <- summary(pca_size)$importance

# Loadings of the PCs
summ_pca_load_size <- pca_size$rotation

For the size-corrected PCA, we used only penguins with all three beak measurements and tarsus length (n = 83), compared with 92 penguins in the original PCA, because tarsus length is also missing for some individuals.

Show the code 
# OWNER: Maria
# Table of variance explained by each PC, original and size-corrected PCA
tibble(PC                = colnames(summ_pca_var_nonsize),
       orig_var          = summ_pca_var_nonsize["Proportion of Variance", ]*100,
       orig_cum          = summ_pca_var_nonsize["Cumulative Proportion", ]*100,
       size_var          = summ_pca_var_size["Proportion of Variance", ]*100,
       size_cum          = summ_pca_var_size["Cumulative Proportion", ]*100) %>%
    kable(col.names = c("PC", "Variance (%)", "Cumulative (%)",
                        "Variance (%)", "Cumulative (%)"),
          digits = 1, align = c("l", rep("r", 4))) %>%
    add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Original" = 2, "Size-corrected" = 2)) %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

In both PCAs (original and size-corrected), PC1 and PC2 together explained most of the variation (86.7% in the original and 87.4% in the size-corrected PCA), while PC3 explained little (Table 2).

Show the code 
# Loadings bar chart function: same design for the original and size-corrected PCA
make_loadings_plot <- function(pca, title) {
    # Percentage of variance explained by each PC
    var <- summary(pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100
    # Loadings of PC1 to PC3 in long format
    loadings_long <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation[, c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3")]) %>%
        rownames_to_column("measurement") %>%
        mutate(measurement = c("Culmen length", "Beak width", "Beak depth")) %>%
        pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2, PC3), names_to = "PC", values_to = "loading") %>%
        mutate(PC = paste0(PC, " (", round(var[PC], 1), "%)"))
    # Bars of loadings: measurement on the y-axis, loading on the x-axis
    ggplot(loadings_long, aes(x = loading, y = measurement)) +
        # Grey vertical line at zero to separate positive and negative loadings
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        # One bar per measurement, in grey (color is reserved for genus)
        geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.6) +
        # Loading value at the end of each bar
        geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", loading),
                      hjust = ifelse(loading < 0, 1.15, -0.15)),
                  size = 3.5, color = "grey25") +
        # Let value labels extend past the panel edge instead of being cut off
        coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
        # Same range for all panels, with room for the value labels
        scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.3, 1.3), breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5)) +
        labs(title = title, x = "Loading", y = NULL) +
        # Clean white theme with readable text size
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        # Light vertical gridlines only; bold panel and plot titles
        theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "grey93", linewidth = 0.3),
              strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) +
        # One panel per PC
        facet_wrap(~ PC) 
}

Figure 1 shows the loadings of each beak measurement on the three principal components, and Figure 2 shows the position of each penguin on PC1 and PC2, for both the original and the size-corrected PCA.

p_load_orig <- make_loadings_plot(pca_orig, "Original")
p_load_size <- make_loadings_plot(pca_size, "Size-corrected")

# One above the other, with panel tags A and B
p_load_orig / p_load_size + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

We ran the LDA on the same log-transformed beak measurements as the original PCA (Table 3) and on the size-corrected measurements (Table 4), to check whether genera remain separated once body size is removed.

Show the code 
# OWNER: Stephanie
# Linear discriminant analysis: how well can genus be predicted from the beak.
# It uses the same four log beak measurements (predictors) as the PCA, plus genus 
# (grouping variable to predict)
# MASS package does lda

# Leave-one-out cross-validation (CV = TRUE): each penguin is classified by a model fitted without that penguin, so the accuracy isn't over-optimistic
lda_cv <- MASS::lda(x = pca_dta[, pca_vars_log],
                    grouping = droplevels(pca_dta$genus),
                    CV = TRUE)

# table of actual vs predicted genus: table(actual, predicted) - no figure?, 
# we already will have two figures (PCA + loadings)
# % correct overall and per genus
actual <- droplevels(pca_dta$genus)
predicted <- lda_cv$class

#   Table of actual vs predicted genus (rows = actual, columns = predicted)
cm <- table(actual, predicted)

#   % correct overall
overall_pct <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm) * 100
       #equivalent: mean(predicted == actual) *100

#   % correct per genus (diagonal / row total, because rows = actual)
per_genus_pct <- diag(cm) / rowSums(cm) * 100

# make the table print with footnote of accuracy
cm_tbl <- cbind(as.data.frame.matrix(cm),
                `% correct` = per_genus_pct)
kable(cm_tbl, digits = 2) %>%
    kable_styling() %>%
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) %>%
    kableExtra::footnote(general = paste0("Overall accuracy: ", round(overall_pct, 1), "%"),
                         general_title = "")
Show the code 
# OWNER: Stephanie
# LDA, using the size-corrected data
# Predictors: residuals of each log beak measurement on log tarsus length

# Leave-one-out cross-validation, as above
lda_cv_size <- MASS::lda(x = beak_resid,
                         grouping = droplevels(pca_size_dta$genus),
                         CV = TRUE)

# Actual vs predicted genus
actual_size    <- droplevels(pca_size_dta$genus)
predicted_size <- lda_cv_size$class

# Table of actual vs predicted genus (rows = actual, columns = predicted)
cm_size <- table(actual_size, predicted_size)

# % correct overall
overall_pct_size <- sum(diag(cm_size)) / sum(cm_size) * 100

# % correct per genus
per_genus_pct_size <- diag(cm_size) / rowSums(cm_size) * 100

# Table with % correct per genus and overall accuracy as a footnote
cm_tbl_size <- cbind(as.data.frame.matrix(cm_size), `% correct` = per_genus_pct_size)
kable(cm_tbl_size, digits = 2) %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) %>%
    kableExtra::footnote(general = paste0("Overall accuracy: ", round(overall_pct_size, 1), "%"), general_title = "")
Show the code 
# Biplot function: same design for the original and size-corrected PCA
make_biplot <- function(pca, genus, labels, title, arrow_scale = 2.5) {
    # Percentage of variance explained by each PC
    var <- summary(pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ] * 100
    # PC1 and PC2 scores of each penguin, with its genus
    scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) |> mutate(genus = genus)
    # Loadings, stretched so the arrows are visible next to the points
    arrows <- as_tibble(pca$rotation[, 1:2] * arrow_scale) |>
        mutate(measurement = c("Culmen", "Width", "Depth"),
               # Mostly horizontal arrow (TRUE) or mostly vertical (FALSE)
               horiz = abs(PC1) >= abs(PC2),
               # Label just beyond the arrow tip
               lab_x = PC1 * 1.06,
               lab_y = PC2 * 1.06,
               # Horizontal: text starts at the tip and runs outwards;
               # vertical: text centred on the arrow
               hjust = ifelse(horiz, ifelse(PC1 < 0, 1, 0), 0.5),
               # Horizontal: the higher label is nudged up and the lower one down,
               # so labels of arrows pointing the same way do not overlap;
               # vertical: label above or below the tip
               vjust = ifelse(horiz,
                              ifelse(PC2 >= mean(PC2[horiz]), 0.2, 0.8),
                              ifelse(PC2 < 0, 1, 0)))

    ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
        # Grey lines at zero (centre of each PC)
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
        # Penguins as points, colored, shaped and sized by genus
        geom_point(aes(color = genus, shape = genus, size = genus)) +
        # Arrows from the centre to each beak measurement's loading
        geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
                     arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")),
                     color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.7) +
        # Measurement names next to the arrow tips, with a white halo (no box);
        # force = 0 keeps them exactly where placed
        ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = arrows,
                                 aes(x = lab_x, y = lab_y, label = measurement,
                                     hjust = hjust, vjust = vjust),
                                 size = 3.5, color = "grey25", fontface = "bold",
                                 bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.15,
                                 force = 0, force_pull = 0, segment.color = NA,
                                 seed = 1) +
        # # Rounded white box with the genus name (right edge at label_x)
        # geom_label(data = labels,
        #            aes(x = label_x, y = label_y,
        #                label = paste0(genus, "     "), color = genus),
        #            hjust = 1, fontface = "italic", size = 3.4, fill = "white",
        #            label.r = unit(0.5, "lines"),
        #            label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")) +
        # Genus symbol at the right end inside the box
        # geom_point(data = labels,
        #            aes(x = label_x - 0.17, y = label_y,
        #                color = genus, shape = genus, size = genus)) +
        # Genus colors, shapes and sizes (same in every figure)
        scale_color_manual(values = genus_cols) +
        scale_shape_manual(values = genus_shapes) +
        scale_size_manual(values = genus_sizes) +
        # Legend in two columns 
        guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
               shape  = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
               size   = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
        # Same limits in both panels so they have the same shape and align;
        # equal scale on both axes so distances are not distorted
        coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.2, 4.2), ylim = c(-4.2, 2.5), clip = "off") +
        # Panel title and axis titles with % of variance
        labs(title = title,
             x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var["PC1"], 1), "%)"),
             y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var["PC2"], 1), "%)"),
             color = "Genus", shape = "Genus", size = "Genus") +
        # Clean theme, light grid, no legend
        theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
        theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey93", linewidth = 0.3),
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
              legend.title = element_blank(),
              legend.position = "inside",
              legend.position.inside = c(1.04, 0.02),
              legend.justification = c(1, 0),
              legend.text = element_text(face = "italic"),
              legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
              legend.margin = margin(4, 6, 4, 6))
}

Discussion

Principal components. Our PCAs showed that penguin beak variation is organised along two largely distinct dimensions, both before and after size correction (Figure 1; Table 2): beak thickness/robustness (PC1, dominated by beak width and depth) and beak length (PC2, almost entirely determined by culmen length). Although we expected that PC1 would reflect overall beak size, culmen length contributed little to PC1 (-0.18), and even less after size correction (-0.06). This means that penguins with thicker beaks do not necessarily have longer beaks. This suggests that beak length and thickness may have evolved somewhat independently across penguins, possibly in relation to different feeding demands, although our data cannot test this directly. Because PC1 and PC2 explained most of the variation, the biplots (Figure 2) show only these two components.

Original PCA. Some genera form distinct groups in the biplot (Figure 2 A). Aptenodytes separates along the culmen length arrow, indicating longer beaks, while Eudyptula lies opposite the width and depth arrows (narrower, shallower beaks). Eudyptes lies in the direction of the width and depth arrows (wider, deeper beaks). Pygoscelis, Spheniscus and Megadyptes overlap in the centre. Because this PCA was not corrected for size, the extreme positions of the largest (Aptenodytes) and smallest (Eudyptula) penguins may partly reflect body size.

Size-corrected PCA. After removing the effect of body size, the same overall pattern remains, although the groups are less compact and overlap more (Figure 2 B). Aptenodytes still lies along the culmen length arrow, but closer to the centre, which suggests that its long beak is partly, but not only, explained by its large size. Eudyptula still lies opposite the width and depth arrows, so its beak remains relatively narrow and shallow for its size, and Eudyptes still lies towards wider, deeper beaks. The LDA supports this pattern: genus was correctly predicted for 89.1% of penguins with the original measurements and still for 83.1% after size correction (Table 3; Table 4), so differences in beak shape between genera are not simply a consequence of body size. The exception is the group of Pygoscelis, Spheniscus and Megadyptes, which continue to overlap in the centre; no Megadyptes penguin was correctly classified, most being assigned to Spheniscus.

Question 2: Does the hand-wing index still vary among penguin genera?

Introduction

The variable focused on in this question is the hand-wing index, which measures how elongated a bird’s wing is. It is calculated as Kipp’s distance (the distance from the tip of the first secondary feather to the tip of the longest primary feather) divided by the total wing length, multiplied by 100. Ecologists commonly use it as a single-number proxy for flight efficiency and dispersal ability, with higher values indicating longer, more pointed wings (Sheard et al., 2020).

Penguins are flightless and use their wings primarily as flippers. We are asking whether this trait, normally tied to flight, still differs between genera or has become similar across the group. If differences remain, they may reflect differences in flipper shape related to how each group swims and forages. To answer the question, we compare the hand-wing index among the six penguin genera, and we use tarsus length as a proxy for body size to explore possible reasons for any differences.

Approach

To address our question we made two plots of different types. Figure 3 is a boxplot of the hand-wing index for each genus, with every penguin overlaid as a jittered point, colored and shaped by genus, and the sample size (n) shown under each genus name. A boxplot is a good fit because it shows the median, spread and outliers of a numeric variable across several groups at once, and the jittered points keep the raw data visible, so genera with few penguins are not hidden behind a box. Figure 4 is a scatterplot of the hand-wing index against tarsus length (a proxy for body size), with points colored and shaped by genus. A scatterplot is the best choice for showing the relationship between two numeric variables, and coloring by genus shows whether any trend reflects differences between genera.

To check the visual impression, we tested whether the hand-wing index differs among genera. Because Bartlett’s test indicated unequal variances across genera, we used Welch’s ANOVA, which does not assume equal variances, followed by Games-Howell pairwise comparisons to identify which genera differ. Since some genera have only four penguins, we also ran a Kruskal-Wallis test as a robustness check; if both tests agree, our conclusion does not depend on the choice of test. As the effect size we report omega-squared, which is less biased than eta-squared for small groups and estimates the proportion of variation in hand-wing index explained by genus. Finally, to explore possible reasons for any differences, we compared the mean Kipp’s distance and wing length of each genus (Table 7) and the correlation between the hand-wing index and tarsus length (Spearman’s rank correlation).

Analysis

Show the code 
# OWNER: Andrew
# Filter out missing values
q2_data <- penguins |>
    filter(!is.na(hwi), !is.na(genus))

# summary per genus: n, mean, sd, median, 95% CI of the mean
q2_summary <- q2_data |>
    group_by(genus) |>
    summarise(
        n       = n(),
        mean    = mean(hwi),
        sd      = sd(hwi),
        median  = median(hwi),
        se      = sd / sqrt(n),
        ci_low  = mean - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
        ci_high = mean + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(mean))

q2_summary %>%
    mutate(ci = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", ci_low), " – ", sprintf("%.2f", ci_high))) %>%
    select(genus, n, mean, sd, median, ci) %>%
    kable(col.names = c("Genus", "n", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "95% CI"),
          digits = 2, align = c("l", rep("r", 5))) %>%
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE) %>%
    kable_styling()

The number of penguins with a hand-wing index ranged from 4 to 29 per genus, and mean values ranged from 3.70 (Aptenodytes) to 7.10 (Megadyptes) (Table 5).

Show the code 
# OWNER: Andrew
# Welch's ANOVA (main test), Games-Howell post hoc, omega-squared effect size,
# Kruskal-Wallis as a robustness check

# assumption checks (why Welch rather than standard ANOVA)
q2_shapiro <- q2_data |>
    group_by(genus) |>
    filter(n() >= 3) |>
    summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(hwi)$p.value)

q2_bartlett <- bartlett.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)

# main test: Welch's ANOVA (does not assume equal variances)
q2_welch <- oneway.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data, var.equal = FALSE)

# post hoc: which genera differ
q2_gh <-rstatix::games_howell_test(q2_data, hwi ~ genus)

# effect size: omega-squared
fit <- aov(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)
ss  <- summary(fit)[[1]]
omega_sq <- (ss[1, "Sum Sq"] - ss[1, "Df"] * ss[2, "Mean Sq"]) /
    (sum(ss[, "Sum Sq"]) + ss[2, "Mean Sq"])

# robustness check: Kruskal-Wallis (no normality assumption)
q2_kw <- kruskal.test(hwi ~ genus, data = q2_data)

Because variances differed among genera (Bartlett’s test, p = 0.038), we used Welch’s ANOVA, which does not assume equal variances. The hand-wing index differed among genera (F = 14.1, p <0.001), with a large effect size (ω² = 0.39). Although Shapiro-Wilk tests did not detect departures from normality in any genus, these tests have little power with so few penguins per genus, so we also ran a Kruskal-Wallis test, which does not assume normality; it gave the same result (H = 33.9, p <0.001). Pairwise comparisons (Games-Howell) identified 5 pairs of genera that differed significantly (Table 6).

Show the code 
# OWNER: Andrew
# Significant pairwise comparisons, with the higher-index genus listed first

q2_gh |>
    filter(p.adj < 0.05) |>
    # Swap genera when the difference is negative, so all differences are positive
    mutate(higher  = if_else(estimate > 0, group2, group1),
           lower   = if_else(estimate > 0, group1, group2),
           diff    = abs(estimate),
           ci_low  = if_else(estimate > 0, conf.low, -conf.high),
           ci_high = if_else(estimate > 0, conf.high, -conf.low),
           ci      = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", ci_low), " – ", sprintf("%.2f", ci_high)),
           p_adj   = format.pval(p.adj, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    arrange(desc(diff)) |>
    select(higher, lower, diff, ci, p_adj) |>
    kable(col.names = c("Higher index", "Lower index", "Difference", "95% CI", "Adjusted p"),
          digits = 2, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
    column_spec(1:2, italic = TRUE)

Figure 3 shows the distribution of the hand-wing index in each genus.

Show the code 
# OWNER: Stephanie
# Exploratory checks for possible reasons why the hand-wing index varies 
# Body size: Spearman correlation between hwi and tarsus_length
# exact = FALSE because tied values prevent an exact p-value
size_cor <- cor.test(q2_data$hwi, q2_data$tarsus.length,
                     method = "spearman", exact = FALSE) 

# Components of the index: mean kipps_distance and wing_length per genus
q2_components <- q2_data |>
  group_by(genus) |>
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    mean_kipps  = mean(kipps.distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_wing   = mean(wing.length, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hwi    = mean(hwi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # ratio of the two means: a quick check that it tracks mean hwi
  mutate(kipps_wing_ratio = 100 * mean_kipps / mean_wing) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_hwi))

# Sex: number of female, male and unknown-sex penguins per genus, to check
# whether any genus is dominated by one sex (reported in the Discussion). 
q2_sex <- q2_data |>
  group_by(genus) |>
  summarise(
    F_n = sum(sex == "F", na.rm = TRUE),
    M_n = sum(sex == "M", na.rm = TRUE),
    U_n = sum(sex == "U", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # % male among penguins of known sex
    pct_male = 100 * M_n / (F_n + M_n),
    dominated = case_when(pct_male >= 70 ~ "mostly male",
                          pct_male <= 30 ~ "mostly female",
                          TRUE ~ "balanced")
  )

# This table shows comparing mean Kipp’s distance and wing length across genera 
# to see which part of the hand-wing index drives any differences between them.
kable(
    q2_components,
    col.names = c("Genus", "Penguins", "Mean Kipp's distance",
                  "Mean wing length", "Mean hand-wing index",
                  "100 × Kipp's / wing"),
    digits = 2,
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
    column_spec(1, italic = TRUE)

The hand-wing index was significantly correlated with tarsus length (Spearman’s \(\rho\) = -0.4, p <0.001; Figure 4). Table 7 shows the mean Kipp’s distance and wing length of each genus, the two components of the hand-wing index.

Maria Sans-Fuentes: Claude (Anthropic) was used to:

  • debug R code, for example how to print the variance explained from a PCA summary with kable() (using summary(pca)$importance) and why missing color values removed all points from a ggplot;
  • place the labels in the PCA biplots (it helped me write the code that positions the measurement names just beyond the end of each loading arrow, keeping the names of arrows that point in the same direction from overlapping, and suggested starting positions for the genus labels, which I then adjusted by hand after checking the rendered figure).
  • help configure the document to render in HTML, PDF and Word. This included choosing a package (flextable) that builds the tables in all three formats and adding table of contents for each format.
  • how to display very small p-values as “< 0.001” instead of scientific notation using teh base fucntion `format.pval, which was not rendering correctly in the report).

Footnotes

  1. PCA combines several related measurements into a few new axes, called principal components (PCs), which capture most of the variation in the data. This allows us to summarize the beak measurements in two-dimensional plots.↩︎

  2. Allometry refers to the way body parts change in proportion to overall body size; for example, larger penguins tend to have larger beaks. These relationships are usually curved on the original scale but become linear after a log transformation. Logging also makes differences between small and large penguins proportional.↩︎

  3. LDA finds the combinations of measurements that best separate predefined groups (here, genera), and then uses them to assign each penguin to the genus it most resembles.↩︎

  4. Each penguin is classified by a model fitted without that penguin, so the accuracy is not over-optimistic.↩︎
